title: BambooToken Linux Malware Uses MQTT to Run Shell Commands and Steal Files
content_md: Researchers have analyzed a Linux malware sample identified as BambooToken, a backdoor that uses the MQTT messaging protocol for command-and-control (C2) communications. The malware can collect system information, execute shell commands, browse files, upload data, and steal files from compromised Linux machines . The analyzed sample is a stripped, statically linked 64-bit Linux ELF file with the SHA-256 hash bf0681e43f51e98fe7ec24bf73a43facc66b0feb325a3a835f8f01b2861b926e . Its hash is listed in Black Lotus Labs’ published BambooToken Linux indicators, supporting the malware-family attribution. However, the available evidence does not independently identify the operator behind the activity. BambooToken contains an encrypted 59-byte configuration blob that reveals its MQTT infrastructure after decoding. The malware uses a single-byte XOR key to recover the broker hostname live-hk[.]c2iznja[.]com and a hard-coded group topic, {534E19D5-434B-4cad-A0C2-8D75E0B2FBFC} . BambooToken Linux MQTT Backdoor The malware connects to the MQTT broker over TCP port 2883. It creates a new UUID-like client identifier during execution, allowing the attacker to communicate with each infected system through a distinct MQTT topic. If the connection fails, BambooToken waits 15 seconds before retrying. The malware can also run in the background using a double-fork daemonization routine. This detaches it from the terminal, changes its working directory to / , and sets its file-creation mask to zero. R
